10: If the Tzomet haGiddim (the convergence of sinews, the term being related to [Song 4:3] mibaad l'tzamatekh/ from behind your mass of hair) is missing or severed - it's treif, even if the whole bone is intact.

Tzomet haGiddim occur on a beast on the middle bone (tibia) on its outside such that the tail falls upon it. But there's an opinion that it's on the inside facing the cavity.

Rema: And it's proper to be strict and follow both views (B"Y ...) but the first view is the main one (which is the view of Rashi, Tesefot, Rosh and gedolei France and Germany).

They begin above the Arkum (talus, astragalus, ankle bone, knucklebone) which is the small bone that connects the Shuk (tibia) to the Arkuba ("knee;" metatarsals) that is sold with the head. This is the bone that children play with and it's called "Koril," and above it these sinews attach and converge, ascending and spreading out on the Shuk until they become soft and go back to looking like flesh.
If it's severed or absent facing the Arkum it's kosher. Above the Arkum which is where the butchers hang it - it's treif.

Their length is from where they start converging, up to where they spread out in the flesh of large catttle, 16 thumbreadths, but there's someone who says it's 4 breadths, and in small beasts the Sages gave no length except their appearance and texture, for as long as they're white, hard and thick they have the rule of Tzomet haGiddim. But where they start turning soft or they're small and fine they don't have the rule of Tzomet haGiddim. And where they're not so white but just somewhat white and they glisten like glass it wouldn't be Tzomet haGiddim.
There are other Giddim, sinews, that are enveloped inside these like male inside female, but these are not included in the category of Tzomet haGiddim.

The Tzomet haGiddim in a beast are three: one thick one and two thin ones. If just the thick on is severed it's permitted since behold two remain. If both the thin ones are severed it's permitted since behold the thick one is bigger than them together so behold the whole Tzomah only missing a minority of it. If the majority of all of them is severed it's treif (verb. Rambam Shechita 8:18)

Rema: The thick sinew is the one that they part when they hang the beast and it lies over the two, and they're stick to the flesh and bone (Morekhai in the name of Rabya).
In a bird they are on the middle bone [drumstick] like on a beast, 16 of them, and if the majority of one of them is severed it's treif (Ramban and Ran).

The sign that shows where the Tzomet haGiddim ends, is the same in a bird as in small beasts.

Rema: And whoever is versed in determining its span, can measure any bird in proportion to its size. Wherever it's hard it's Tzomet haGiddim and wherever it's soft it's not Tzomet haGiddim (Piskei Mharai #141). And whoever is not versed in measuring it, should measure by a thumbreadth in a bird from where it starts (ibid. per Maharil) but Tzomet haGiddim is never longer than half your middle finger (Rokeach #404). But we are not versed in measuring Tzomet haGiddim in birds because it's hard to check and easily treiffed, therefore whenever there's a wound at the Tzomet haGiddim, even if it's just swollen and bruised, since it would need checking and we're not versed in birds - it's treif (Mordekhai ...).

If the bone broke at the Tzomet haGiddim then it mended and healed well there are those that permit it if the appearance of the flesh that's over the fracture is unaltered, but some forbid it until he checks the Tzomet haGiddim (which is the main opinion, and for us who are not versed in checking birds it's treif) (Rosh ...).
